<form class="book-practice" id="quiz-p07" data-practice-set="P07" novalidate>
<p id="quiz-p07-instructions">Choose one answer for each of the 10 questions. Complete the set, then select <strong>Check answers</strong> to see your score and explanations. Each question is worth one point.</p>
<noscript><p>For a self-check without JavaScript, record your choices, then open the answer key below.</p></noscript>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-01" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">1.</span> A service team is choosing between adding reminders and simplifying its application form. Which finding most strongly favors simplifying the form first?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-a" name="p07-01" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Users complete the form easily when a reminder arrives before the deadline.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-b" name="p07-01" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Users report that they planned to apply but forgot the closing date.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-c" name="p07-01" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Users repeatedly return but stop at a field they cannot interpret.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-d" name="p07-01" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Users complete the form quickly after a colleague mentions the service.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-e" name="p07-01" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Users rarely open the existing reminder because it arrives during the night.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-01-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-02" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">2.</span> Two people accept the same rain forecast but choose different policies about carrying an umbrella. Which additional information is most relevant before judging either policy mistaken?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-a" name="p07-02" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Whether the two people discussed the forecast before making their choices</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-b" name="p07-02" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> How many other people chose to carry an umbrella that day</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-c" name="p07-02" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> How each person values carrying the umbrella and getting wet</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-d" name="p07-02" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Whether the forecast is displayed as a percentage or as odds</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-e" name="p07-02" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Which forecasting service has the best reputation among their friends</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-02-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-03" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">3.</span> One intervention sends a reminder at the intended action time. Another is a voluntarily chosen restriction preventing access to a competing activity. Which distinction is correct?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-a" name="p07-03" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Both are informational defaults.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-b" name="p07-03" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Both establish that a habit has already formed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-c" name="p07-03" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> The first removes choice; the second only changes wording.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-d" name="p07-03" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-e" name="p07-03" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-03-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-04" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">4.</span> A panel&#x27;s recorded estimates disagree with an AI forecast. Which evidence would most strongly justify assigning the AI greater weight for this type of decision?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-a" name="p07-04" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Closer agreement with panel estimates after members review the AI&#x27;s explanation</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-b" name="p07-04" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> More detailed explanations of the variables contributing to the AI forecast</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-c" name="p07-04" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Higher confidence scores accompanying the AI&#x27;s most recent predictions</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-d" name="p07-04" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Better fit to the historical cases used to develop the forecasting system</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-e" name="p07-04" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Lower error than the panel’s independent forecasts on comparable held-out cases</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-04-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-05" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">5.</span> A redesigned application page increases submissions but also increases processing delays and ineligible applications. Which outcome is most useful for deciding whether to retain it?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-a" name="p07-05" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Satisfaction ratings collected immediately after a form is submitted</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-b" name="p07-05" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> The proportion of applicants who return to check their submission status</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-c" name="p07-05" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Net benefit from services delivered after counting processing and applicant costs</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-d" name="p07-05" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> The number of submitted applications per visitor to the redesigned page</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-e" name="p07-05" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The time users spend locating and pressing the submission button</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-05-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-06" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">6.</span> A team has resources to pilot a new decision aid while continuing the current workflow. Which design best isolates the aid&#x27;s effect on the same predefined performance measure?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-a" name="p07-06" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Compare the aided team&#x27;s performance with a historical industry benchmark.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-b" name="p07-06" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Compare volunteers who adopt the aid with colleagues who prefer the current workflow.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-c" name="p07-06" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Ask experienced managers to assess how plausible the aid&#x27;s recommendations appear.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-d" name="p07-06" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Compare performance before and after the whole team switches to the new aid.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-e" name="p07-06" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows during the same period.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-06-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-07" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">7.</span> A reader wants to make routine exercise more enjoyable at the time it occurs. Which arrangement uses temptation bundling?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-a" name="p07-07" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Set aside money that will be forfeited if the weekly target is missed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-b" name="p07-07" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Display a reminder beside the door before the usual exercise time.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-c" name="p07-07" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Record each completed session on a chart shared with a friend.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-d" name="p07-07" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Watch a favorite film after completing the week&#x27;s full exercise target.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-e" name="p07-07" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Reserve a favorite entertainment podcast for listening during exercise.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-07-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-08" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">8.</span> A model recommends denying a request, but its training labels reflect past administrative decisions that may contain errors. What is the most important governance step?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-a" name="p07-08" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-b" name="p07-08" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-c" name="p07-08" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-d" name="p07-08" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-e" name="p07-08" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-08-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-09" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">9.</span> A protective action costs 3 and prevents an event loss of 20 completely. There are no other effects. Group A has event probability 0.1 and group B 0.3. Under expected-loss minimization, which policy fits?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-a" name="p07-09" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-b" name="p07-09" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Act for neither group.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-c" name="p07-09" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Act for A only.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-d" name="p07-09" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Act for B only.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-e" name="p07-09" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Act for both groups.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-09-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-10" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">10.</span> A program has one available place and the same cost for either recipient. Reliable causal estimates say it reduces A&#x27;s event risk from 40% to 35% and B&#x27;s from 25% to 10%. If the sole objective is to maximize expected events prevented, who should receive the place?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-a" name="p07-10" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Neither, because risk is not reduced to zero.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-b" name="p07-10" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> B, because the expected reduction is 15 percentage points.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-c" name="p07-10" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A, because treated risk remains 35%.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-d" name="p07-10" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> A, because baseline risk is 40%.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-e" name="p07-10" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Either, because the program costs the same.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-10-result" hidden></p></fieldset>

<details class="practice-key" id="answers-p07"><summary>Answers and explanations</summary><ol class="practice-answer-list">
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p07-01"><h3>Question 1: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Users complete the form easily when a reminder arrives before the deadline. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This suggests that a prompt can help initiate an otherwise feasible action.</dd>
<dt>B. Users report that they planned to apply but forgot the closing date. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Forgetting the deadline makes reminders a more direct candidate.</dd>
<dt>C. Users repeatedly return but stop at a field they cannot interpret. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Repeated attempts combined with a specific comprehension barrier point to task difficulty rather than a missing prompt.</dd>
<dt>D. Users complete the form quickly after a colleague mentions the service. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Successful completion after a prompt provides little evidence of a form-comprehension barrier.</dd>
<dt>E. Users rarely open the existing reminder because it arrives during the night. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This points toward the timing of the prompt rather than the form&#x27;s difficulty.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a>. <a href="#p07-01">Back to question 1</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p07-02"><h3>Question 2: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Whether the two people discussed the forecast before making their choices <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Discussion history does not establish the relevant costs and benefits of either action.</dd>
<dt>B. How many other people chose to carry an umbrella that day <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The majority&#x27;s policy does not establish what is best for either person&#x27;s circumstances.</dd>
<dt>C. How each person values carrying the umbrella and getting wet <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Different consequences can justify different action thresholds under the same probability forecast.</dd>
<dt>D. Whether the forecast is displayed as a percentage or as odds <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Equivalent displays do not determine which consequences each person should prefer.</dd>
<dt>E. Which forecasting service has the best reputation among their friends <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The stem already gives a shared forecast; source reputation does not settle differences in the value of acting.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-02">Back to question 2</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-03"><h3>Question 3: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Both are informational defaults. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Neither necessarily preselects a menu option.</dd>
<dt>B. Both establish that a habit has already formed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>An intervention is not evidence of learned automaticity.</dd>
<dt>C. The first removes choice; the second only changes wording. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses their practical effects.</dd>
<dt>D. The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The reminder does not mandate, and the restriction changes choices.</dd>
<dt>E. The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A reminder supplies a cue, while a restriction changes later feasible behavior.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a>. <a href="#p07-03">Back to question 3</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-04"><h3>Question 4: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Closer agreement with panel estimates after members review the AI&#x27;s explanation <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Agreement after exposure can reflect anchoring and does not validate either forecast independently.</dd>
<dt>B. More detailed explanations of the variables contributing to the AI forecast <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Detailed explanations may help inspection without establishing predictive performance.</dd>
<dt>C. Higher confidence scores accompanying the AI&#x27;s most recent predictions <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Self-reported confidence requires calibration against outcomes before it can justify greater weight.</dd>
<dt>D. Better fit to the historical cases used to develop the forecasting system <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Fit on development data can overstate predictive performance on new decisions.</dd>
<dt>E. Lower error than the panel’s independent forecasts on comparable held-out cases <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A fair comparison uses information available at the time of each forecast. Relevant out-of-sample performance then provides a basis for weighting the forecasts without relying on confidence or presentation.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-04">Back to question 4</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p07-05"><h3>Question 5: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Satisfaction ratings collected immediately after a form is submitted <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Immediate experience omits later delays, eligibility outcomes, and service delivery.</dd>
<dt>B. The proportion of applicants who return to check their submission status <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Return visits can reflect uncertainty or delays rather than improved welfare.</dd>
<dt>C. Net benefit from services delivered after counting processing and applicant costs <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The decision needs a downstream benefit measure that accounts for burdens as well as the rise in activity.</dd>
<dt>D. The number of submitted applications per visitor to the redesigned page <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Conversion measures the proximal action but omits the downstream consequences.</dd>
<dt>E. The time users spend locating and pressing the submission button <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Faster interaction does not establish that services reach eligible applicants efficiently.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-05">Back to question 5</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-06"><h3>Question 6: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Compare the aided team&#x27;s performance with a historical industry benchmark. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Differences in case mix and conditions can explain a gap from the benchmark.</dd>
<dt>B. Compare volunteers who adopt the aid with colleagues who prefer the current workflow. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Adoption choices can be related to ability, motivation, or the cases staff handle.</dd>
<dt>C. Ask experienced managers to assess how plausible the aid&#x27;s recommendations appear. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Expert plausibility ratings do not isolate its effect on the predefined performance measure.</dd>
<dt>D. Compare performance before and after the whole team switches to the new aid. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Other changes over time can contribute to the observed difference.</dd>
<dt>E. Randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows during the same period. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Random allocation and contemporaneous comparison help separate the aid&#x27;s effect from case selection and changing conditions.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-06">Back to question 6</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-07"><h3>Question 7: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Set aside money that will be forfeited if the weekly target is missed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This is a commitment penalty rather than pairing exercise with a tempting activity.</dd>
<dt>B. Display a reminder beside the door before the usual exercise time. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This supplies a prompt rather than an enjoyable experience during the task.</dd>
<dt>C. Record each completed session on a chart shared with a friend. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Monitoring and social accountability differ from bundling the activity with an immediate temptation.</dd>
<dt>D. Watch a favorite film after completing the week&#x27;s full exercise target. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This is a later contingent reward, rather than enjoyment bundled with performing the activity.</dd>
<dt>E. Reserve a favorite entertainment podcast for listening during exercise. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The enjoyable activity is paired with the beneficial task, supplying an immediate reason to begin and continue it.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a>. <a href="#p07-07">Back to question 7</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p07-08"><h3>Question 8: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Sample size does not establish label validity.</dd>
<dt>B. Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Predictions can reproduce historical judgments; authorization and correction remain human responsibilities.</dd>
<dt>C. Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Presentation cannot repair a flawed target.</dd>
<dt>D. Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Confidence does not validate the target or fairness standard.</dd>
<dt>E. Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This blocks correction of consequential mistakes.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-08">Back to question 8</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p07-09"><h3>Question 9: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The threshold is 3/20 = 0.15, not one half.</dd>

Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 10 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#p07-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** A service team is choosing between adding reminders and simplifying its application form. Which finding most strongly favors simplifying the form first?

A) Users complete the form easily when a reminder arrives before the deadline.
B) Users report that they planned to apply but forgot the closing date.
C) Users repeatedly return but stop at a field they cannot interpret.
D) Users complete the form quickly after a colleague mentions the service.
E) Users rarely open the existing reminder because it arrives during the night.

:::

::: {#p07-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** Two people accept the same rain forecast but choose different policies about carrying an umbrella. Which additional information is most relevant before judging either policy mistaken?

A) Whether the two people discussed the forecast before making their choices
B) How many other people chose to carry an umbrella that day
C) How each person values carrying the umbrella and getting wet
D) Whether the forecast is displayed as a percentage or as odds
E) Which forecasting service has the best reputation among their friends

:::

::: {#p07-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** One intervention sends a reminder at the intended action time. Another is a voluntarily chosen restriction preventing access to a competing activity. Which distinction is correct?

A) Both are informational defaults.
B) Both establish that a habit has already formed.
C) The first removes choice; the second only changes wording.
D) The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction.
E) The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device.

:::

::: {#p07-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** A panel's recorded estimates disagree with an AI forecast. Which evidence would most strongly justify assigning the AI greater weight for this type of decision?

A) Closer agreement with panel estimates after members review the AI's explanation
B) More detailed explanations of the variables contributing to the AI forecast
C) Higher confidence scores accompanying the AI's most recent predictions
D) Better fit to the historical cases used to develop the forecasting system
E) Lower error than the panel’s independent forecasts on comparable held-out cases

:::

::: {#p07-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** A redesigned application page increases submissions but also increases processing delays and ineligible applications. Which outcome is most useful for deciding whether to retain it?

A) Satisfaction ratings collected immediately after a form is submitted
B) The proportion of applicants who return to check their submission status
C) Net benefit from services delivered after counting processing and applicant costs
D) The number of submitted applications per visitor to the redesigned page
E) The time users spend locating and pressing the submission button

:::

::: {#p07-06 .practice-question}
**Question 6.** A team has resources to pilot a new decision aid while continuing the current workflow. Which design best isolates the aid's effect on the same predefined performance measure?

A) Compare the aided team's performance with a historical industry benchmark.
B) Compare volunteers who adopt the aid with colleagues who prefer the current workflow.
C) Ask experienced managers to assess how plausible the aid's recommendations appear.
D) Compare performance before and after the whole team switches to the new aid.
E) Randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows during the same period.

:::

::: {#p07-07 .practice-question}
**Question 7.** A reader wants to make routine exercise more enjoyable at the time it occurs. Which arrangement uses temptation bundling?

A) Set aside money that will be forfeited if the weekly target is missed.
B) Display a reminder beside the door before the usual exercise time.
C) Record each completed session on a chart shared with a friend.
D) Watch a favorite film after completing the week's full exercise target.
E) Reserve a favorite entertainment podcast for listening during exercise.

:::

::: {#p07-08 .practice-question}
**Question 8.** A model recommends denying a request, but its training labels reflect past administrative decisions that may contain errors. What is the most important governance step?

A) Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous.
B) Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route.
C) Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process.
D) Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair.
E) Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model.

:::

::: {#p07-09 .practice-question}
**Question 9.** A protective action costs 3 and prevents an event loss of 20 completely. There are no other effects. Group A has event probability 0.1 and group B 0.3. Under expected-loss minimization, which policy fits?

A) Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5.
B) Act for neither group.
C) Act for A only.
D) Act for B only.
E) Act for both groups.

:::

::: {#p07-10 .practice-question}
**Question 10.** A program has one available place and the same cost for either recipient. Reliable causal estimates say it reduces A's event risk from 40% to 35% and B's from 25% to 10%. If the sole objective is to maximize expected events prevented, who should receive the place?

A) Neither, because risk is not reduced to zero.
B) B, because the expected reduction is 15 percentage points.
C) A, because treated risk remains 35%.
D) A, because baseline risk is 40%.
E) Either, because the program costs the same.

:::

::: {#answers-p07 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: C.**

- **A. Users complete the form easily when a reminder arrives before the deadline. (Incorrect)** This suggests that a prompt can help initiate an otherwise feasible action.
- **B. Users report that they planned to apply but forgot the closing date. (Incorrect)** Forgetting the deadline makes reminders a more direct candidate.
- **C. Users repeatedly return but stop at a field they cannot interpret. (Correct)** Repeated attempts combined with a specific comprehension barrier point to task difficulty rather than a missing prompt.
- **D. Users complete the form quickly after a colleague mentions the service. (Incorrect)** Successful completion after a prompt provides little evidence of a form-comprehension barrier.
- **E. Users rarely open the existing reminder because it arrives during the night. (Incorrect)** This points toward the timing of the prompt rather than the form's difficulty.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd). [Back to question 1](#p07-01).

**Question 2: C.**

- **A. Whether the two people discussed the forecast before making their choices (Incorrect)** Discussion history does not establish the relevant costs and benefits of either action.
- **B. How many other people chose to carry an umbrella that day (Incorrect)** The majority's policy does not establish what is best for either person's circumstances.
- **C. How each person values carrying the umbrella and getting wet (Correct)** Different consequences can justify different action thresholds under the same probability forecast.
- **D. Whether the forecast is displayed as a percentage or as odds (Incorrect)** Equivalent displays do not determine which consequences each person should prefer.
- **E. Which forecasting service has the best reputation among their friends (Incorrect)** The stem already gives a shared forecast; source reputation does not settle differences in the value of acting.

Review: [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 2](#p07-02).

**Question 3: E.**

- **A. Both are informational defaults. (Incorrect)** Neither necessarily preselects a menu option.
- **B. Both establish that a habit has already formed. (Incorrect)** An intervention is not evidence of learned automaticity.
- **C. The first removes choice; the second only changes wording. (Incorrect)** This reverses their practical effects.
- **D. The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction. (Incorrect)** The reminder does not mandate, and the restriction changes choices.
- **E. The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device. (Correct)** A reminder supplies a cue, while a restriction changes later feasible behavior.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd). [Back to question 3](#p07-03).

**Question 4: E.**

- **A. Closer agreement with panel estimates after members review the AI's explanation (Incorrect)** Agreement after exposure can reflect anchoring and does not validate either forecast independently.
- **B. More detailed explanations of the variables contributing to the AI forecast (Incorrect)** Detailed explanations may help inspection without establishing predictive performance.
- **C. Higher confidence scores accompanying the AI's most recent predictions (Incorrect)** Self-reported confidence requires calibration against outcomes before it can justify greater weight.
- **D. Better fit to the historical cases used to develop the forecasting system (Incorrect)** Fit on development data can overstate predictive performance on new decisions.
- **E. Lower error than the panel’s independent forecasts on comparable held-out cases (Correct)** A fair comparison uses information available at the time of each forecast. Relevant out-of-sample performance then provides a basis for weighting the forecasts without relying on confidence or presentation.

Review: [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 4](#p07-04).

**Question 5: C.**

- **A. Satisfaction ratings collected immediately after a form is submitted (Incorrect)** Immediate experience omits later delays, eligibility outcomes, and service delivery.
- **B. The proportion of applicants who return to check their submission status (Incorrect)** Return visits can reflect uncertainty or delays rather than improved welfare.
- **C. Net benefit from services delivered after counting processing and applicant costs (Correct)** The decision needs a downstream benefit measure that accounts for burdens as well as the rise in activity.
- **D. The number of submitted applications per visitor to the redesigned page (Incorrect)** Conversion measures the proximal action but omits the downstream consequences.
- **E. The time users spend locating and pressing the submission button (Incorrect)** Faster interaction does not establish that services reach eligible applicants efficiently.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 5](#p07-05).

**Question 6: E.**

- **A. Compare the aided team's performance with a historical industry benchmark. (Incorrect)** Differences in case mix and conditions can explain a gap from the benchmark.
- **B. Compare volunteers who adopt the aid with colleagues who prefer the current workflow. (Incorrect)** Adoption choices can be related to ability, motivation, or the cases staff handle.
- **C. Ask experienced managers to assess how plausible the aid's recommendations appear. (Incorrect)** Expert plausibility ratings do not isolate its effect on the predefined performance measure.
- **D. Compare performance before and after the whole team switches to the new aid. (Incorrect)** Other changes over time can contribute to the observed difference.
- **E. Randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows during the same period. (Correct)** Random allocation and contemporaneous comparison help separate the aid's effect from case selection and changing conditions.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 6](#p07-06).

**Question 7: E.**

- **A. Set aside money that will be forfeited if the weekly target is missed. (Incorrect)** This is a commitment penalty rather than pairing exercise with a tempting activity.
- **B. Display a reminder beside the door before the usual exercise time. (Incorrect)** This supplies a prompt rather than an enjoyable experience during the task.
- **C. Record each completed session on a chart shared with a friend. (Incorrect)** Monitoring and social accountability differ from bundling the activity with an immediate temptation.
- **D. Watch a favorite film after completing the week's full exercise target. (Incorrect)** This is a later contingent reward, rather than enjoyment bundled with performing the activity.
- **E. Reserve a favorite entertainment podcast for listening during exercise. (Correct)** The enjoyable activity is paired with the beneficial task, supplying an immediate reason to begin and continue it.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd). [Back to question 7](#p07-07).

**Question 8: B.**

- **A. Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous. (Incorrect)** Sample size does not establish label validity.
- **B. Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route. (Correct)** Predictions can reproduce historical judgments; authorization and correction remain human responsibilities.
- **C. Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process. (Incorrect)** Presentation cannot repair a flawed target.
- **D. Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair. (Incorrect)** Confidence does not validate the target or fairness standard.
- **E. Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model. (Incorrect)** This blocks correction of consequential mistakes.

Review: [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 8](#p07-08).

**Question 9: D.**

- **A. Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5. (Incorrect)** The threshold is 3/20 = 0.15, not one half.
- **B. Act for neither group. (Incorrect)** For B the expected benefit exceeds the cost.
- **C. Act for A only. (Incorrect)** This reverses the comparison of avoided loss with cost.
- **D. Act for B only. (Correct)** Expected avoided losses are 2 for A and 6 for B; only B exceeds the cost 3.
- **E. Act for both groups. (Incorrect)** For A the certain cost exceeds the expected avoided loss.

Review: [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 9](#p07-09).

**Question 10: B.**

- **A. Neither, because risk is not reduced to zero. (Incorrect)** Partial risk reduction still serves the stated objective.
- **B. B, because the expected reduction is 15 percentage points. (Correct)** B's estimated benefit exceeds A's five-point reduction.
- **C. A, because treated risk remains 35%. (Incorrect)** Remaining risk does not measure the benefit of treatment.
- **D. A, because baseline risk is 40%. (Incorrect)** Highest baseline risk is not the same as greatest preventable risk.
- **E. Either, because the program costs the same. (Incorrect)** Equal cost does not erase the unequal benefits.

Review: [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 10](#p07-10).
